{{short description|Fixed-point theorem in algebraic geometry}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Borel fixed-point theorem''' is a [[fixed-point theorem]] in [[algebraic geometry]] generalizing the [[Lie–Kolchin theorem]]. The result was proved by {{harvs |txt |authorlink=Armand Borel |first=Armand |last= Borel |year=1956}}.

==Statement==
If ''G'' is a [[connected space|connected]], [[solvable group|solvable]], linear [[algebraic group]] [[Algebraic geometry#Regular functions|acting regularly]] on a [[non-empty]], [[complete variety|complete]] [[algebraic variety]] ''V'' over an [[algebraically closed field]] ''k'', then there is a [[Group action (mathematics)#Fixed points and stabilizer subgroups|''G'' fixed-point]] of ''V''.

The Lie-Kolchin theorem proves this result under the stronger hypothesis that ''V'' is a [[projective variety]].

A more general version of the theorem holds over a field ''k'' that is not necessarily algebraically closed. A solvable algebraic group ''G'' is ''split over k'' or ''k-split'' if ''G'' admits a [[composition series]] whose composition factors are isomorphic (over ''k'') to the [[additive group]] <math>\mathbb G_a</math> or the [[multiplicative group]] <math>\mathbb G_m</math>. If ''G'' is a connected, ''k''-split solvable algebraic group acting regularly on a complete variety ''V'' having a [[rational point|''k''-rational point]], then there is a ''G'' fixed-point of ''V''.<ref>Borel (1991), Proposition 15.2</ref>
